$comment: The shared conformance corpus: language-neutral test vectors every Mantle Place host
plugin runs against its own parser. Seeded from the Unreal reference suite, which had
them as inline C++ string literals reachable by exactly one host.
NORMATIVE: this corpus is one third of an MPB spec release (schema + spec/ prose +
corpus, versioned together) - a conforming reader passes it. This file is data; what
claiming a group obliges a reader to is spec/conformance.md, the additional first-party
plugin obligations are the Host Plugin Standard's (HPS-40, HPS-41), and the integrity
checks the CI gate applies are check_manifest_conformance.py's. Nothing here restates them.
Case fields:
id              stable, dotted, never renumbered — host suites name it in failures.
group           manifest | vault | auth | cache | digest | projection.
file            path relative to corpus/.
expect          accept  — the parser MUST accept and produce `expectations`.
reject  — the parser MUST refuse; `errorContains` if the message matters.
A reject case MAY still carry `expectations` for values the
parser is required to have read BEFORE refusing (HPS-37).
vector  — a known-answer table, not a single document to parse.
reason          why the case exists. Required: a fixture nobody can explain gets
deleted the first time it is inconvenient.
appliesTo       this case asserts ONE host's manifest block; other hosts skip it
(HPS-41). Absent means host-invariant.
expectations    derived values a conformant host must produce (optional).
errorContains   substring the refusal message must contain (optional).
malformedJson   this file is deliberately not valid JSON (optional).
manifestVersion the bundle-manifest version this case's file carries (optional). Checked
by check_manifest_conformance.py against the file's own `version` field —
a case whose declared and actual versions disagree is corpus rot, caught
before any host suite sees it.
Top-level fields:
corpusVersion   the shape of THIS index's case fields — bumped on a breaking change to
what a field means, not on adding cases. Each host pins the corpusVersion
it was last reviewed against in verified-against.json
(`verifiedAgainstCorpusVersion`); check_manifest_conformance.py fails a
host that trails this number.
manifestVersion the bundle-manifest version this corpus's fixtures are written against.
OWNERSHIP: maintainer-owned. A host that needs a new case proposes it here by pull
request rather than forking a private copy.

cases.reason: The loopback redirect is attacker-reachable. The empty-expected-state case is the one that matters: a host that treats ''=='' as a match accepts any callback.

PKCE is the one place where a plausible-looking implementation is silently insecure. The RFC 7636 Appendix B pair proves S256 end to end; the base64url triples catch the padding and +/ substitution bugs that make a verifier fail server-side.

Whether a failed refresh discards the stored credential or keeps it. The two failure modes are not symmetric: reading a transient failure as definitive costs a working session to a dropped packet, while reading a definitive rejection as transient retries a dead credential at every launch and never prompts the sign-in that would fix it. Only the second is silent. Host-invariant deliberately - the codes are a platform contract, and a host that honours a fifth spelling locally has forked it.

Transcribed as data so a .NET or Python host can drive the identical table instead of re-deriving the guards. The unchanged-by-default rule is what keeps an out-of-order callback from corrupting the session.
expires_in <= 0 and the refresh-token-preservation rule are both silent-failure classes: one logs the user out instantly, the other on the next restart.
An order id is attacker-influencable text that becomes a filesystem path. Traversal neutralisation and collision resistance are both required, and they pull in opposite directions.
The null-sha256 row is the whole reason this table is in the corpus: 'unknown' and 'corrupt' look identical to a naive implementation and have opposite correct responses.
NIST FIPS 180-4 known answers. Two hosts already had to ship their own SHA-256 because the platform primitive was unusable; these pin any future one.
A base bundle carries no host block yet. It is not importable, but bbox/layout/order_id MUST still be parsed so streaming and the vault join key survive — the early return must not skip them.
buildings_mesh carries no hash of its own; the host resolves it by matching path against the top-level buildings.formats[] entry. Cross-block resolution, not convention.

Regression guard: the pre-history anonymous `dcc_readiness.mesh_import` is RETIRED — readiness lives at `hosts.<hostId>.readiness` — and a stray one must be ignored, never used as a fallback. A fallback ladder here is how a clean break quietly becomes dual-parsing (HPS-31).

Readiness is per host, at `hosts.<hostId>.readiness`. The host reads its OWN subtree and surfaces the stated reason instead of dead-ending on an empty import. The sibling host's block must be ignored, not merged.

v19 closes `reason` into #/$defs/deliveryReason, and closing it required GROWING the set: `not_produced` and `not_selected` did not exist through v18. A host that matches on the reason instead of surfacing it (HPS-36) loses the explanation on exactly the values v19 added. Pairs with manifest.dccReadinessReason, which pins a value that predates v19.

`hosts.revit` is ANOTHER host's block. This fixture states the two georeferences in conflict on purpose — `hosts.unreal.georeference` is metric UTM, `hosts.revit.georeference` a State Plane foot zone — so a reader that keys placement off whichever it finds first reports 2231 and fails. HPS-33: apply your own block, never merge or re-derive from a sibling.

v19 publishes the Revit deliverables' sha256 inside the `revit` block and NOWHERE else — `elevation.points_csv` and `buildings.ifc` still carry none. A host that keeps reading the hash off the v18 detail block surfaces three unverifiable artifacts while every other assertion stays green, which is the hole this case exists to close. HPS-33: read your OWN block, verbatim.

The mirror of manifest.revitBlockIgnored, pointed the other way: this fixture states THREE origins in conflict on purpose — `hosts.unreal.georeference.origin.utm` (metric UTM), `delivery.local_origin` (metric UTM, host-neutral) and `hosts.revit.georeference.origin.projected` (State Plane feet) — and Revit must report the one addressed to it. Before it had a block of its own this host had only `delivery.local_origin`, emitted on the `local_ft` tier ALONE, so a metric-tier bundle carried no survey point and the model was imported not georeferenced at all; reading the own block as PRIMARY with delivery as the fallback is what closes that without a coordinated pipeline release. Note `grid_rotation_deg` is deliberately non-zero. The emitters reproject per-vertex so today's bundles publish 0.0, and a fixture that agreed would be passed by a host that hardcodes zero and never reads the field — the value is here to be carried, not to be plausible. `linear_unit` is on the ORIGIN and differs from the artifacts' own `units` on this tier, which is the pair a host must not collapse: reading a State Plane foot origin as metres places the site 3.28× out.
The drape carries the same required-sha rule as the heightmap.

The reference accept shape, lifted from the platform's reference fixture. A host that parses this correctly has the whole `hosts.unreal` block, its `readiness` verdicts and the placement math covered. It carries `landscape_layers` in full: all eight sub-blocks, each with its source raster's hash and its UE-ready PNG companions, whose `value_mapping` shape follows the companion's `encoding`. The companions are declared 143x142 against a 1009-post heightmap deliberately - the weight rasters ride the DEM's grid, not the Landscape's, so a host that assumes the two match is wrong. Every placement tuple here (landscapeScale, landscapeSpawnLocation, drapeWorldRect*) is in the HOST ENGINE's axis order, which for Unreal is left-handed North=+X / East=+Y. The manifest names its own grid axes the other way round (`scale_x_percent` and `component_count_x` describe EASTING), so these tuples read as swapped against the source fields on purpose — that swap is the thing under test. Mapping East to +X instead swaps two axes of a Z-up frame, which is a reflection rather than a rotation, and mirrors the whole import.
The heightmap sha256 has been required since v17 and remains so — refuse to import unverifiable bytes.
The mesh sha256 is OPTIONAL: absent means the integrity check is skipped, which is 'unknown', not 'absent'. This is the asymmetry hosts get wrong.

A glTF pointer declaring an up axis the importer does not convert must fail closed, the way planet_shape does. Every consumer that trusts its glTF reader's fixed Y-up-to-Z-up conversion has this exposure: the bundle would import at a plausible-looking transform, rotated, with no error anywhere - the worst failure shape there is. The value must be READ before the refusal (HPS-37) so the message can name what it got. `nanite_recommended` rides along to prove the refusal happens on the axis and not on a half-parsed block.

The counterpart to manifest.planetShapeSphere: ABSENT is not a rejection. The flat frame is the default, so a bundle that simply omits the field imports. A host that fails closed on absence rejects most real bundles.

Only the flat frame is supported in v1. An unknown planet_shape fails closed rather than silently importing a wrong frame. The value must be READ before the refusal (HPS-37) so the message can name what it got.
Unparseable bytes must fail closed with a manifest-shaped error, not crash.

The schema lists `sha256` in the `required` set of every `hosts.revit.*` deliverable it publishes, so a present block without one is a producer bug. A host that keeps treating it as optional imports unverifiable bytes and reports them as fine — the asymmetry HPS-34 draws between a hash that was never published (skipped, valid-but-unverified) and one that was promised and is missing (refuse).
An absent `version` reads as 0, which is below the floor. Absence is not a licence to guess.
Clean break: v13 predates the MPB 1.0.0 floor and MUST be refused outright, not best-effort parsed.
Clean break: v14 predates the MPB 1.0.0 floor and MUST be refused outright, not best-effort parsed.
Clean break: v16 predates the MPB 1.0.0 floor and MUST be refused outright, not best-effort parsed.

Clean break: v17 was the supported version until the v18 hygiene bump and is now refused like any other old version. Nothing about the shape changed enough to matter — the point is that 'nearly current' gets no special treatment.
Clean break: v6 predates the MPB 1.0.0 floor and MUST be refused outright, not best-effort parsed.
Clean break: v7 predates the MPB 1.0.0 floor and MUST be refused outright, not best-effort parsed.

component_count_x * (sections_per_component * section_size_quads) + 1 MUST equal resolution. 4*126+1 = 505, not 512 — an internally inconsistent manifest is a producer bug and must not be papered over.
Layer selection is by name AND format — a decoy `road` layer and a sibling gpkg must both lose to road_splines/geojson.
No geojson means no splines. A host must not fall back to a format it cannot read.

HPS-47: 'is this bundle materialized' is decided from the neutral signals (a non-empty `hosts` object, or a non-empty vector.layers array), never from a host's own content. The other-host and unknown-host rows catch a host keying off its own block — the coincidence found holding up the road-splines cases, made a rule.

The lon/lat <-> UTM known-answer pin. A host that gets the false northing or the zone wrong places geometry kilometres away while every test that does not check numbers still passes — the definition of a silent failure.
No url means no download. Fail closed and surface the platform's own message.
Presigned URL + expiry. The URL is minted per import and never cached past expiry.

The presign REQUEST, which nothing asserted until a host shipped an empty body and a schema rejection came back as two unactionable words. The route validates its body, so there is no default; and the whole-bundle token must be named as itself, never through the deprecated 'glb' alias whose meaning depends on whether the order happens to carry a glb artifact. Every existing download case pins the RESPONSE, which is why a host asking for the wrong thing stayed green.

ONE precedence order for every platform error-body parser, auth and vault alike (HPS-48) — the split this case used to document is resolved. The competing-key vectors pin the order; the machine-readable `code` (refunded / revoked on a 410) is a separate read that drives UI and is unaffected.
An empty vault is a successful response, not an error.

null means UNKNOWN, not absent and not zero. The legacy row must survive with every `has…` companion false — a host that coerces null to 0 will later claim a size mismatch against a bundle it never knew the size of.

items.layersNote: elevation is known-and-FALSE. A host that reads 'layers object present' as 'all three true' passes a laxer check and is wrong.
items.downloadFormatsNote: byteSize 0 means UNRECORDED, not an empty file — a host that hides zero-size formats hides half the download menu.

items.layersNote: layers is null: nothing is known, and no flag may be read.
items.valuesNote: manifestVersion / sizeBytes / sha256 are deliberately absent here: the row's nulls mean UNKNOWN, so there is no value to assert, only hasX=false.

cases.reason: THE malformed-row rule: skip the bad row, keep the good ones, warn. One unparseable entry must never blank a customer's whole vault.

The tier label is ONE host's answer: its whole discriminator is the presence of `glb` — the Unreal terrain mesh — so it cannot ride a host-invariant case (HPS-41). Three rows for the three branches: empty formats is UNKNOWN (the base_on_demand marker, which advertises nothing yet), formats without `glb` is Base, and `glb` present is the full Unreal set. A host that collapses the first two loses the difference between 'nothing is known' and 'known to be partial' — which is the difference between materializing and importing.
A missing `bundles` array is a contract violation, not an empty vault. Failing closed here is what stops 'your vault is empty' from being a lie.
THE single-flight 409 shape. Recognised by BODY, not by status code, and reported as SUCCESS — the caller joins the running job instead of erroring or starting a second.
Normal start: a fresh jobId.
A materialize-start body with no job id fails closed and surfaces the platform's message via the HPS-48 precedence. Fails closed today in the reference; asserted nowhere before this case.

Nothing left to build is a SUCCESS that names no job. The platform answers this way when everything asked for is already delivered, or when the rest can never be produced for this area. A host that reads the absence of a job id as a failure refuses the one response meaning 'your bundle is ready' — and where the download only happens past this parse, that host cannot import at all.

The order's core build has not finished, so the picks are parked and fire on their own when it does. Also a success with no job: there is nothing to poll YET, and telling the curator to retry would queue nothing and explain less.
The 200-flavoured join. It carries `activeJobId` and NO `jobId`, so a host keying on `jobId` alone sees 'no id' on a request that succeeded and joined a running build.

A single-flight refusal may report the running job WITHOUT naming it — `activeJobId` is null. This is still a join, not an error: polling is keyed on the ORDER, not the job (the status request never took a job id), so an unnamed run is fully followable. A host that refuses here tells a curator to retry a build that is already going, which is the failure HPS-24 exists to prevent.

Polling this endpoint returns a DELIVERY-STATE document — delivered / notDelivered / activeJob — with no status word anywhere, so completion is derived rather than read. This table is that derivation. It is also the more truthful reading: a run reports `completed` even when every token's emit failed, so delivery is proof of production and a job status is not.

What a NEW request would still have to ask for, derived alongside the state. The state word alone is not actionable: `Pending` is the wire shape of BOTH “the job row is not visible yet” (wait) and “the run this host joined has ended without building what it needs” (ask again), and a reader that cannot separate them polls out its whole budget on the second. Scoped to unreal because it is the only host that acts on it today — the Revit host has the same Pending fall-through and should claim this case when it grows a re-pick.
Status-word synonym buckets and progress normalisation. Every host maps a different vocabulary onto the same five states; this table is that mapping.

The reference host's token list, shown as the SHAPE a host must send: an explicit array it owns. The server-side `"unreal"` keyword expands to only four core tokens and would silently drop the vector and landcover layers — which is exactly why the list is client-owned. Each host substitutes its own tokens; only the shape is normative.

Unparseable vault-listing bytes must fail closed, not crash and not blank the vault. The manifest group had this fixture from day one; the vault parser relied on a host-local assertion until this case landed.
The wire vocabulary is wider than the state set. Hosts that switch on exact strings silently drop bundles when the platform adds a synonym.

Clean break: v18 — the per-host dcc_readiness hygiene bump — predates the MPB 1.0.0 floor and MUST be refused outright, not best-effort parsed. The integer era is pre-history now; a host reads the version's JSON TYPE and refuses the whole family below its floor (HPS-31). Re-procurement, not dual-parsing, is how a bundle at rest crosses the break.

Clean break: v19 — the last version of the integer pre-history — predates the MPB 1.0.0 floor and MUST be refused outright, not best-effort parsed. The integer era is pre-history now; a host reads the version's JSON TYPE and refuses the whole family below its floor (HPS-31). Re-procurement, not dual-parsing, is how a bundle at rest crosses the break.

Semver near-miss: the integer era's 19 spelled as a JSON STRING. The families are told apart by JSON type, so "19" is not the pre-history — it is a malformed MPB version and MUST be refused. A reader that coerces it through a number resurrects dual-parsing across the era break.
Semver near-miss: "1.0" is not MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH. A permissive parser that pads the missing component invents a version the platform never published — refusal, not repair.
Semver near-miss: MPB publishes no pre-release tags, so "1.0.0-rc1" MUST fail the parse and be refused. A reader that strips the tag imports against a contract that does not exist.

Semver near-miss: semver forbids a leading zero and the platform's publisher and gate enforce it, so "01.0.0" MUST be refused. Both first-party hosts accepted it until a test caught the drift — this case is what keeps it caught, for every host at once.

`hosts.unreal.foliage_points` publishes a sha256 and a point_count, and both were read by nothing: the tree-points CSV was the ONE payload an importer brought in unverified while every other one rode the integrity chain. Both facts live in THIS host's block on purpose -- the same values also sit under `landcover.tree_points`, addressed to nobody in particular, and a host bound to its own block (HPS-33) cannot reach them there. The case pins that the CSV is in the set of payloads a conformant reader verifies before it writes anything, which is the claim the integrity chain makes and could not previously honour.

The same block with neither optional fact. Both are OPTIONAL in the schema because they come from a best-effort sidecar, so their absence is UNKNOWN and never CORRUPT (format.md section 5): the bundle still imports, the digest check is skipped rather than failed, and no row count is cross-checked. The third state is the one hosts collapse -- reporting this payload as verified is a lie, and reporting it as corrupt makes every sidecar-less bundle un-importable.

`point_count` against the rows a reader really produced. The digest and the count answer different questions: sha256 proves the bytes, the count proves the rows this reader made of them. Skipping a malformed row is correct -- one bad row must not drop the layer -- and it is exactly what turns a column-contract drift into a shorter table whose digest still matches. A declared count of 0 means unknown and cross-checks nothing, which is the row a reader treating it as 'expect zero rows' fails.

`imagery_drape.alignment` is a FREE STRING the schema says to match on its PREFIX, because the divergent shape embeds the ETL's measured figures. Left opaque, a partially-covering drape imports silently misaligned and the failure looks like nothing at all. The import PROCEEDS -- the UV transform already rides the declared extents, so the placement is right and only the user is missing a fact -- and the reader surfaces the covered percentage and the overshoot ratio it read out of the sentence. Anchored reads, not positional ones: the figures are pinned so a reader that echoes the string without parsing it fails here.

expectations.drapeAlignment: diverges from heightmap extent (imagery covers 68.9% of the heightmap, overshoot 1.12×)

cases.reason: The shape the ETL emits when it had no heightmap extent to compare against. It is not a warning and not a defect: nothing is known, so nothing is claimed. A reader that treats every non-matching shape as a problem cries wolf on this one, and a reader that treats it as 'matches' claims a check the producer said it could not perform.

A fourth shape, from a producer newer than the reader. The descriptor is informational -- nothing about the import transform is decided from it -- so an unrecognised value is echoed opaquely and the bundle imports (compatibility.md section 3). Refusing here would make every additive minor a breaking release, and branching only on the shapes a reader knows shows a user nothing at all for the shape it does not.

expectations.drapeAlignment: clipped to heightmap extent (a shape published after this plugin version)

cases.reason: The bundle declares its imagery matches the heightmap extent while its own two rectangles say it covers about half of it. Nothing is re-derived to catch this -- both rectangles are published values and the reader only asks whether the bundle's claim about them is true. It is the one alignment case that fails CLOSED, because a bundle whose own numbers refute its own claim imports looking correct and is silently mis-draped, which is the failure that looks like nothing. The slack is 1%: the reference bundle's imagery is ~0.1% short of its AOI and truthfully says 'matches', so a reader comparing exactly refuses a good bundle.
